world.title: Ethiopia Renews IFAD Partnership, Increases Contribution Tenfold
world.description:
Addis Ababa, September 25, 2026 (ENA) —Ethiopia has reaffirmed its longstanding partnership with the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD), increasing its contribution to the Fund’s 14th Replenishment (IFAD14) tenfold.
President Taye Atske-Selassie made the commitment during a high-level gathering attended by African Heads of State and Government, United Nations Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed and IFAD President Alvaro Lario.
The renewal commitment came as Ethiopia steps up efforts to transform rural livelihoods and strengthen agricultural development.
President Taye highlighted Ethiopia’s nearly five-decade partnership with IFAD, which has supported efforts to improve the livelihoods and resilience of millions of people across the country’s rural and pastoralist communities.
 
Through successive programmes, the partnership has reached nearly 10 million people, backed by 227 million USD in national contributions and approximately 1.2 billion USD in total co-financing.
Demonstrating Ethiopia’s renewed commitment to the partnership, the government has increased its contribution to IFAD14 from 100,000 USD to 1 million USD, a tenfold increase.
The move underscores Ethiopia’s continued focus on rural transformation, agricultural development and strengthening opportunities for rural and pastoralist communities, it was learned.

science.title: Beyond conventional performance assessment of recycled aggregate concrete through integrated data analytics
science.description: The mechanical performance of recycled aggregate concrete (RAC) varies with aggregate quality, mixture composition, and experimental conditions, complicating the interpretation of published replacement-ratio trends. This study integrates descriptive statistics, LOWESS smoothing, bootstrap uncertainty estimation, derivative-based analysis, and clustering to examine five normalized indicators: compressive strength, splitting tensile strength, flexural strength, bulk density, and elastic modulus. Property-specific complete-case analyses cover RCA replacement ratios from 0 to 100%. The fitted relationships indicate overall reductions relative to the reference mixtures, together with property-specific non-monotonic features. Elastic modulus exhibits the largest between-category effect-size estimate, whereas bulk density shows comparatively small absolute changes in normalized response. The maximum-absolute-slope locations differ among properties and do not consistently represent deterioration: the NCS location occurs on a local upward segment of the bootstrap-mean curve. These locations and the associated high-slope intervals are therefore interpreted as method-dependent descriptors rather than physical failure thresholds. Four fixed RCA intervals provide an exploratory description of the compiled evidence, without defining safe replacement limits or structural application classes. The framework supports transparent synthesis and hypothesis generation, while source heterogeneity, within-study dependence, uneven coverage, and sensitivity to the analytical specification limit broader inference.

science.title: Integrated genome and RNA sequencing analysis as a powerful technical framework to diagnose primary ciliary dyskinesia
science.description: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) is a rare, genetically heterogeneous respiratory disorder. Exome sequencing results unsuccessful in almost 30% of patients, likely due to variants in noncoding regions or structural variants. We applied RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) on epithelial nasal tissue in combination with Genome Sequencing (GS) as a second-tier strategy. Total RNA was extracted from 29 genetically undiagnosed PCD cases (study group), 8 genetically solved cases and 15 healthy participants. Ciliary enrichment was assessed before analysis of aberrant expression, aberrant splicing and monoallelic expression. GS was also performed in the study group. Ciliary transcriptome was robustly captured in 88% of the samples. Causative RNA alterations were identified in all samples from the positive control group. In the study group, causative transcriptomic outliers were detected in 22% of families, and the integration of GS increased the molecular diagnostic yield to 30% of families. A range of transcriptomic alterations was observed in association to their underlying causative variants, including single-nucleotide variants, copy number variants, and an insertion of a LINE element, most of them being novel. The affected genes included FOXJ1, CCDC40, RSPH1, CFAP54, SPAG1, HYDIN and AK8. In conclusion, the combination of GS and RNA-seq constitute a valuable diagnostic strategy for PCD.

science.title: New study opens doors for precise control of cells using light
science.description:
Researchers at the Texas A&M Health Institute of Biosciences and Technology have developed a tool using a simple light to manipulate proteins and microtubules in the cells of the body, giving researchers new ways to observe progression and implications of complex diseases like cancer and dementia.
The study, published in Cell Reports Methods, was led by Yubin Zhou, MD, PhD, FAAAS, FAIMBE, FRSC, director of the Center for Translational Cancer Research at the Institute of Biosciences and Technology and professor in the Texas A&M Naresh K. Vashisht College of Medicine, together with Yun Huang, PhD, FRSC, professor and associate director of the Center for Epigenetics and Disease Prevention.

science.title: Prehistoric Sharks Resurface After 325 Million Years: Scientists Stunned By The Discovery
science.description: Inside the twisting tunnels of Mammoth Cave, the world’s largest cave system, scientists have uncovered fossilized remains of two ancient shark species that once prowled Earth’s waters some 325 million years ago. These newly identified fossils were found in Kentucky’s Mammoth Cave as well as in northern Alabama, offering a rare glimpse into a world that existed long before dinosaurs ever appeared.

science.title: Tiny Microbes in Tree Bark
science.description: In addition to storing carbon through photosynthesis, trees have another carbon cycle trick up their sleeve, or rather, bark, and it's been hiding in plain sight. Scientists recently discovered that tree bark hosts millions of microbes involved in consuming and producing methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. Biogeochemist and forest ecologist Jonathan Gewirtzman of Yale University, who was not part of the study published in the journal Science, has been studying the relationship between trees and microbes, and he spoke with Living on Earth’s Jenni Doering.
